text:
- The marketing machine banks every winning hook, then expands with adjacent angles that mirror proven phrasing.
- Personalization pillars: availability, speed, personalization, and volume—use them as vocabulary cues, not as hook templates.
- Hooks set the promise; follow-up assets deliver proof, nurture, and CTA later in the sequence.
- Respect word economy: 6-14 words, conversational, and anchored to concrete outcomes.

- Hooks sell the next five seconds; meats and CTAs happen later in the assembly line.
- 70-20-10 allocation keeps winners in rotation while testing new angles.
- Build hooks in batches, then select the top performers before pairing with body copy.
- Reuse winning lines, adjust 20% to explore adjacent promises, and reserve 10% for bold experiments.
- Each hook must stand alone with one promise, active verbs, and zero CTA leakage.

- Statement hooks declare a sharp benefit; question hooks earn curiosity; commands push decisive action; conditionals frame "if this, then that"; story seeds tease unfinished drama.
- Most aware prospects want proof you can deliver again; product aware prospects want your differentiator; solution aware wants clarity; problem aware needs pain agitated; unaware needs curiosity or intrigue.
- Banned phrases: cut jargon like "unlock your potential" and mushy verbs that weaken the promise.
- Active voice + human rhythm: read aloud before shipping; anything clunky gets cut.
- No multi-idea lines. If you need a conjunction, write a new hook.

- Treat ideation like an assembly line: planner assigns angles, generator drafts fast, editor trims, scorer keeps only the keepers.
- Front-load proof or mechanism words pulled from interviews: "Genie+", "crowd-beater plan", "24-hour blueprint".
- Catalogue hooks with awareness + style tags so future runs reuse high performers intentionally.
- Speed comes from modular roles, not single-pass perfectionism.
